tier_reason: Chapter-05/bench_map_random_access.cpp benchmarks std::map against std::unordered_map, absl and boost maps at 256 and 1024 keys with Google Benchmark, but the repo holds code only; the ns figures are the book's own run relayed by the lead, with a CPU named but compiler, flags and standard library unstated, so first-party C.

corrections.caveats: The numbers are the book's own figures as paraphrased in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere on the repository pages opened (the repo holds the benchmark code and no results, and the Chapter-05 folder has no results files), and the book itself was deliberately not consulted. The data show absl::flat_hash_map and boost::unordered_flat_map are NOT faster than std::unordered_map at these sizes (3.81-4.03 ns versus 3.56-3.81 ns), so the win is hashing versus tree, not the third-party libraries; the book says flat and node variants did not differ because the data fit in cache. Only two tiny, cache-resident sizes; keys are the dense range 0..n-1 inserted in ascending order, and std::hash<int64_t> is the identity in libstdc++ and libc++, so std::unordered_map gets a collision-free best case (and std::map nodes are allocated in key order, which helps its locality). The timed region includes the std::mt19937_64 draw and uniform_int_distribution (a few ns), which compresses the ratios; the generator is seeded from std::random_device, so key sequences differ between runs. Standard library (libstdc++/libc++) and compiler flags not stated; Chapter-05/CMakeLists.txt sets no build type. Tier C: first-party book measurement with the CPU stated but not the flags.

notes: Source matches the record: eight map types, Arg(256) and Arg(1024), operator[] lookups with the RNG draw inside the timed loop. Added the identity-hash, dense-key best case for std::unordered_map and the random_device seeding to caveats. tier_reason: Chapter-04/bench_gemm.cpp times dgemm_basic, dgemm_blocked (block 32) and cblas_dgemm on 1000x1000 doubles with Google Benchmark, but the repo holds code only; the 547/289/24.1 ms figures are the book's own run relayed by the lead, with compiler, flags and CPU unstated, so first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Chapter-04/CMakeLists.txt sets C++20 and no build type or optimisation level; it adds '-g -pg -fno-omit-frame-pointer' to the bench_gemm target only (bench_gemm.cpp, the driver), while dgemm_basic and dgemm_blocked are compiled in the separate static library target 'gemm' (gemm.cpp) without those options. gemm.cpp only compiles with NDEBUG defined (see caveats), which in CMake means a Release, RelWithDebInfo or MinSizeRel build. BLAS comes from CMake FindBLAS (static, 8-byte integers requested, cblas.h from /usr/include/openblas).
corrections.caveats: The numbers are the book's own figures as paraphrased in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere on the repository pages opened (the repo holds the benchmark code and no results, and the Chapter-04 folder has no results files), and the book itself was deliberately not consulted. The only baseline beaten is the book's own naive loop; against the real incumbent (OpenBLAS) the technique is about 12x slower. The -pg/-fno-omit-frame-pointer options apply only to bench_gemm.cpp, not to the gemm library that holds both kernels, so the kernels are not gprof-instrumented. Matrix 'a' is never filled: ct::Matrix uses std::uninitialized_default_construct_n, so its doubles are indeterminate (zero if the allocation came fresh from the OS; leftover data otherwise). dgemm_blocked contains assert(a.is_row_major()) with lowercase names that do not exist, so gemm.cpp only compiles with assertions disabled (NDEBUG), i.e. a Release-type build. Within each 32x32 tile the loop order is still i-j-k with B read down columns; the gain comes from tile reuse in L1, not from a reordered inner loop. The harness does not limit OpenBLAS threads: 24.1 ms for 2e9 flops is about 83 GFLOP/s (derived from the lead's figures), at or above the FP64 peak of one desktop core, so the OpenBLAS row may be multithreaded against single-threaded kernels. The quoted iteration counts times the per-iteration times give about 21 s per benchmark (derived), so the book's run used a non-default --benchmark_min_time or similar that the repo does not record. Compiler and CPU not stated. Tier C: first-party book measurement.

notes: Source matches the record (1000x1000, block 32, alpha 1, beta 0, uninitialised 'a', broken lowercase asserts). Corrected the -pg caveat: it is set on bench_gemm.cpp only, and the kernels live in the separate 'gemm' static library. Added OpenBLAS threading and min_time observations. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 20 stars, last commit 2026-01-22 (active).

tier_reason: Chapter-04/bench_clamp_loop.cpp times ct::clamp_min (std::min) against ct::clamp_conditional on 1,000 uint16_t values with Google Benchmark, but the repo holds code only; the 605 versus 500 ns figures are the book's own run relayed by the lead, with compiler, flags and CPU unstated, so first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated; the lead says GCC assembly is shown. clamp_loop.cpp marks both functions [[gnu::optimize("no-tree-vectorize")]], a GCC-only attribute that Clang ignores; both functions sit in a separate static library (clamp_loop) so they are not inlined into the benchmark. CMakeLists.txt sets C++20 and no build type or optimisation flags.
corrections.caveats: The numbers are the book's own figures as paraphrased in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere on the repository pages opened (the repo holds the benchmark code and no results), and the book itself was deliberately not consulted. With a threshold of 0xFF and uniform uint16_t input, about 99.6% of elements exceed the threshold (derived from the repo constants), so the branch is almost always taken and well predicted: the favourable case for the branchy version, and both versions store almost every element. Vectorisation is switched off for both functions via a GCC-only attribute (a Clang build would vectorise both), which hides the SIMD min a normal -O3 build would use for std::min and makes the comparison unrepresentative of production builds. Each iteration calls PauseTiming/ResumeTiming around a sub-microsecond kernel; Google Benchmark documents these calls as costly, and part of the timer start/stop cost lands in the measured time, so the absolute ns figures overstate the kernel time and the ratio is only indicative. CPU, compiler version and flags not stated. Tier C: first-party book measurement.

notes: Source matches the record (1,000 uint16_t, max 0xFF, refill under PauseTiming, both functions no-tree-vectorize). Added the PauseTiming/ResumeTiming overhead on a ~500 ns kernel and the GCC-only attribute to caveats. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 20 stars, last commit 2026-01-22 (active).
